sub: Technology block (b): handling thousands of live drone tracks without a thousand threads

title: Why Reactive?
desc: Thousands of open connections on a handful of threads — the claim, and where it comes from

items: 1,000 drones × 1 fix per second, and a live map open in 1,000 browsers = 2,000 permanently open connections, each carrying a trickle of data
A blocking stack parks one thread per open connection; threads cost ~1 MB of stack each and the OS scheduler starts to choke around a few thousand
A non-blocking stack keeps a connection open without a thread waiting on it: an event loop of ~one thread per CPU core handles all of them — Spring WebFlux on Project Reactor (Flux, Mono)
Don't take the claim on faith: count the threads of an MVC and a WebFlux build of the same endpoint under the Module 11 load test — that number belongs in your write-up

title: Spring MVC vs. Spring WebFlux
desc: Same annotations on top — a completely different engine underneath

body.alt: Comparison of Spring MVC servlet stack (blocking) and Spring WebFlux reactive stack (non-blocking)
body.caption: MVC: blocking servlet stack (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow). WebFlux: non-blocking reactive stack (adds Netty), plus functional handler & router as an alternative to @Controller.

title: Blocking vs. Reactive: The Same Endpoint Twice
desc: Identical annotation on top — a different machine underneath

body.code: // Spring MVC — one thread held for the whole request @GetMapping("/tracks") List<TrackUpdate> tracks() { return jdbcRepo.findAll(); // blocks the thread at the DB } // WebFlux — the thread is released between elements @GetMapping(value = "/tracks", produces = TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE) Flux<TrackUpdate> tracks() { return r2dbcRepo.findAll(); // non-blocking, streams as SSE }

items: The MVC version holds a servlet thread until the last row arrives — 1,000 live clients means roughly 1,000 threads
The Flux version subscribes; rows flow through the event loop as they arrive — 1,000 clients share a handful of threads
TEXT_EVENT_STREAM turns the endpoint into a live telemetry feed — the moving map in Module 14 consumes exactly this

title: The Reactive Streams Specification
desc: Four interfaces and one crucial idea: backpressure

body.alt: Reactive streams: subscriber subscribes to publisher, subscription mediates request(n) and onNext/onComplete/onError

items: Publisher produces data, Subscriber consumes it, the Subscription mediates
The subscriber controls the flow: request(n) — 'send me at most n elements'
This is backpressure: a slow consumer never gets flooded by a fast producer
Signals: onSubscribe → onNext* → onComplete | onError

title: Core Concepts: Mono & Flux
desc: Two publisher types cover every API you will ever write

body.code: // Mono: 0 or 1 element — a single drone's state Mono<DroneState> state = repository.findById(droneId); // Flux: 0..N elements — the live track stream Flux<TrackUpdate> live = trackService.stream() .filter(t -> t.altitude() < 120) // open category only .sample(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // throttle to 1 Hz .doOnNext(alertService::checkConflicts);

items: Mono — represents 0 or 1 element; Flux — represents an unbounded number of elements
WebFlux router & handlers — functional alternative to Spring MVC controllers (serve live above as a text/event-stream endpoint)
Reactive repositories — non-blocking database access

title: Build the Ingest Handler
desc: POST /drones/{droneId}/fixes from telemetry.yaml (Module 7), reactive end to end — fifteen lines

body.code: private final Sinks.Many<Fix> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); @PostMapping("/drones/{droneId}/fixes") Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> ingest(@PathVariable String droneId, @RequestBody Mono<Fix> body) { return body .filter(f -> f.altMeters() <= 120 && !f.ts().isAfter(Instant.now())) .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new ResponseStatusException(UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY))) // 422 .doOnNext(f -> sink.tryEmitNext(f.withDrone(droneId))) // -> topic later (M9) .thenReturn(ResponseEntity.accepted().build()); // 202 } @GetMapping(value = "/tracks", produces = TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE) Flux<Fix> tracks() { return sink.asFlux() .groupBy(Fix::droneId) .flatMap(perDrone -> perDrone.sample(Duration.ofSeconds(1))); // 1 Hz per drone, not per stream }

body.card: Your task — 30 minutes, then Karate checks it
items: Generate the stub with -g spring --additional-properties=reactive=true (Module 7), paste this in, run it
curl -N localhost:8080/tracks in one terminal; post a fix with altMeters: 38.5 in another — it appears on the stream within a second. Post one with 150 — 422
Why groupBy before sample? Remove it, post fixes for two drones at once, and watch one of them vanish from the stream
Why a Sink and not a List? Because the list is the blocking bug on the next slide

title: Three Ways to Block a Non-Blocking Server
desc: Each of these compiles, passes a unit test, and quietly turns WebFlux back into one-thread-per-request — or worse

body.code: // 1. block() inside the chain — the event-loop thread now waits Flux<Fix> tracks() { return Flux.fromIterable(repo.findAll().collectList().block()); } // 2. a blocking driver on the event loop — JDBC, RestTemplate, File I/O Mono<Zone> zone(String id) { return Mono.just(jdbcTemplate.queryForObject(...)); } // 3. a hot stream with no backpressure policy — memory grows until the JVM dies Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); // unbounded by default!

items: 1. Never block() on a reactive path — return the Flux. Add BlockHound to the test classpath: it throws the moment a blocking call lands on an event-loop thread
2. Use the reactive driver (R2DBC, WebClient) — or, if there is none, subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) to move the call off the loop and be honest that it blocks
3. Telemetry is a stream where the latest value wins: onBackpressureLatest() or sample() at the source; a bounded buffer with onBackpressureBuffer(1000, dropOldest) for anything else
Rule of thumb: if a slow map client can make the ingest endpoint slow, you have coupled them — that is what the topic in Module 9 decouples

title: Tools, Libraries & When to Use It

rows: The reactive foundation under Spring WebFlux
Effortless integration of WebFlux into applications
Reactive database connectivity — replaces blocking JDBC

items: Spring Reactive suits modern, scalable applications
Ideal for microservices, streaming data and high load — i.e. telemetry ingestion, live track distribution, conflict alerting
Not a silver bullet: for simple CRUD services, classic blocking Spring MVC remains simpler to write and debug
